papers.title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI
papers.abstract: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access---giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface.
papers.ranking_reason: It shows how chat interfaces can directly inspect and use the software workspace around them.
papers.explanation: This paper explores giving chat assistants direct access to the app settings and workspace around them. Instead of just reading the text box, the AI can inspect buttons and preferences in a structured way.
papers.why_it_matters: As you build web apps, you will see how hard it is to connect LLMs [large language model, an AI that understands text] to user interfaces. This paper gives you a mental model for how apps can expose their state safely to AI.

project_idea.title: Workspace Inspector Chat
project_idea.description: Write a Python script that lets an LLM read the current state of a local text editor app and answer questions about it. Add a confirmation step so the user must approve any changes the AI wants to make.
project_idea.no_code_version: Use Make.com to connect a Telegram bot to a Google Doc, so the bot can read the current file content and suggest edits back to you.

papers.title: Agent-R^2: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis
papers.abstract: Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R$^2$, a $\textbf{r}$eal-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for $\textbf{r}$ealistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R$^2$ grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R$^2$ distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R$^2$-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R$^2$-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0$\%$ vs. 48.0$\%$) and OfficeQA (14.8$\%$ vs. 13.8$\%$). Further analysis shows that Agent-R$^2$ mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.
papers.ranking_reason: It explains how AI agents can handle realistic daily office work using actual files.
papers.explanation: This paper builds an AI agent that handles real office work by using actual files and multi-format documents. It uses a new training method to stop the AI from rushing through tasks without checking its work properly.
papers.why_it_matters: When building practical AI tools, you need agents that can handle messy folders and files instead of simple text prompts. This paper shows how to train models on real data for better real-world results.

project_idea.title: Local File Organizer Agent
project_idea.description: Build a Python script using an LLM that scans a messy download folder, reads PDFs and text files, and sorts them into correct project subfolders. Add a rule check so it double-checks file contents before moving them.
project_idea.no_code_version: Set up an n8n workflow that triggers when a new file lands in a Google Drive folder, uses AI to summarize it, and moves it to a labeled subfolder.

papers.title: ReferClaw: Disambiguating User Intent for Egocentric Assistance
papers.abstract: Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, "Where did I leave it?" may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. Referclaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.
papers.ranking_reason: It demonstrates an AI assistant that asks clarifying questions when a user's request is unclear.
papers.explanation: This paper introduces an AI assistant that asks clarifying questions when a user gives a vague command. Instead of guessing blindly, the assistant chats with the user to figure out what they mean.
papers.why_it_matters: Users are often vague when talking to AI systems. Learning how to make your bot ask smart follow-up questions instead of failing silently is a great trick for building robust applications.

project_idea.title: Clarifying Chatbot
project_idea.description: Create a Python chatbot that checks if an incoming user request is missing details. If something is unclear, the bot must ask one specific question before running its main task.
project_idea.no_code_version: Build a two-step prompt sequence in an AI workspace tool where the first prompt detects missing information and forces the bot to ask a question.

papers.title: Autonomous AI Agents Systematically Diverge From Human Preferences in Proof Formalization
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have ushered in a new age of proof abundance, but helping humans understand these proofs requires new attention to the differences in how AI agents and humans pursue a proof-making task. We present "simulated collaboration", a methodology that allows us to examine two key questions: (1) the relative attention AI agents pay to surface syntax or, conversely, deeper underlying semantics, and (2) how and where AI agent preferences for what to do next diverge from human preferences. On a set of nine major human collaborations in Lean with 4.7M definitions across more than 6K commits, we find that, over the course of proof construction, AI agents (1) are far more strongly drawn than humans to explicitly marked gaps; (2) show a relative aversion to densely connected proof centers and to complex or surprising proof goals; and (3) are relatively attracted to surprising proof bodies, which they tend to regularize toward baseline. Our results highlight important blind spots and potential interventions for future human-AI collaboration in mathematics.
papers.ranking_reason: It explores how AI preferences differ from human preferences when working together on formal logic.
papers.explanation: This paper compares how human mathematicians write proofs versus how AI agents write them. It finds that AI agents prefer obvious gaps and simple patterns, while humans handle complex core structures differently.
papers.why_it_matters: AI models think differently from humans, especially on strict logic tasks. Knowing these blind spots helps you design better guardrails when AI assists with coding or math.

project_idea.title: Logic Gap Checker
project_idea.description: Write a Python script that compares a human-written code block against an AI-suggested refactor to spot where the AI simplified away complex logic. Print out the differences in a simple report.
project_idea.no_code_version: Use Google Sheets to track different AI prompt outputs for a math problem and manually score them for missing logical steps.

papers.title: Reclassification Is All You Missed: Surfacing Variant Reinterpretation Need in Online Health Communities at Population Scale
papers.abstract: Genetic variants are routinely reclassified in ClinVar after a patient is tested, sometimes from uncertain to pathogenic, yet patient recontact is inconsistent, with no clear duty and responsibility diffused among labs, providers, and patients. Many affected people discuss their results in public online health communities that clinical recontact often does not reach. We built PRISM, an agentic large-language-model pipeline that screens these posts, checks whether the variant was later reclassified, and drafts a disclaimer-bearing outreach message, in a no-contact dry run. Across 3.9 million posts from 32 communities, agent-predicted reinterpretation-relevant discussion is rare (0.288%) but concentrated in specialist genetics communities (6.30% versus 0.10% in general medical-advice communities) and growing fivefold since 2014; PRISM surfaces 123 candidate classification differences, 5 of them from an uncertain submission to pathogenic or likely pathogenic. On a held-out set of 30 real-post drafts, a clinician judged 27 factually grounded and 15 fit to send: factual accuracy is necessary but not sufficient for clinically acceptable outreach. PRISM contributes a population-scale reinterpretation-need map with code and data to be released upon publication.
papers.ranking_reason: It presents an AI pipeline that automatically screens online health communities to help patients.
papers.explanation: This paper presents an AI system that screens online health discussions to find patients whose genetic test results might have changed. It drafts helpful outreach messages while keeping safety and facts in check.
papers.why_it_matters: Handling sensitive medical data requires careful validation and safety checks. This paper shows how to build domain-specific AI pipelines that prioritize factual accuracy over casual guessing.

project_idea.title: Forum Health Disclaimer Bot
project_idea.description: Build a Python script that reads a text file of simulated forum posts, detects medical keywords, and appends a safe disclaimer and summary using an LLM. Log all flagged posts to a CSV file.
project_idea.no_code_version: Connect a Google Form to an AI text analyzer in Make.com that automatically categorizes user feedback and adds a standard safety disclaimer if medical words appear.
